item.title: How Does a Survivor Know She Is Recovering?
item.description:
Trauma

How Does a Survivor Know She Is Recovering?

Healing becomes visible in choices, connection, and purpose.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Recovery is not all-or-nothing; meaningful progress can coexist with distress.
  • Returning to valued activities and setting boundaries can offer ways to recognize change.
  • Working or appearing composed does not rule out a continuing need for professional care.

Natalia was teaching at her school in Kyiv when the mother of one of her students began shouting at her. The confrontation did more than interrupt a lesson. In Natalia’s mind, it brought back the harrowing experience of being in an interrogation room where Russian men were screaming in her face, demanding that she admit to being a spy.

In a later counseling session over Zoom with Ukrainian-American psychotherapist Viktor Dlugunovych, Natalia described how the classroom confrontation made her feel as though she had fallen into a pit of fear. Even so, as memories of her interrogations began to surround her, she interrupted them by closing her eyes, pausing, and reminding herself that she had survived captivity and could get through this encounter, too.

She opened her eyes and calmly told the mother that the conversation would continue in the principal’s office.

The principal, who knew about Natalia’s captivity, later told her that she had expected Natalia to resign. Natalia replied that she had no intention of leaving. Teaching mattered to her, and so did discovering that she could face a frightening moment and decide what to do next.

The incident prompted her to ask once again, “Have I recovered? How do I know when I’ve recovered?”

Dlugunovych explained that distress and progress can coexist. Her flashback was distressing. Yet she was also able to step back from it, set a boundary with the student’s mother, and choose how to respond.

Holding On to an Identity

Natalia is a mathematics and physics teacher with 35 years of classroom experience. She said that during the Russian occupation, authorities kept accusing her of espionage and subjected her to repeated interrogations.

Nightmare Interrogation.
Source: altitudevisual/Adobe Stock

In the interrogation room, she drew on an important part of her identity: her authority as a teacher. Somewhat to her surprise, her young interrogators began treating her with the respect they might have shown one of their own teachers. Their attitudes toward respected authority figures from their past seemed to carry over into how they treated her.

She noticed that the roles seemed to be switching, with her asking questions as a teacher might, rather than simply being questioned and intimidated.

Natalia believes that this respect helped spare her the beatings she said other prisoners endured.

However, captivity still took a severe toll. Natalia described 10 months of sleep deprivation and hunger. Her captors withheld the medication she needed for high blood pressure. They also subjected her to unrelenting verbal abuse, including the shouting that can still trigger flashbacks.

Progress and Pain Can Coexist

Now home and teaching again, Natalia expresses joy at being free in Ukraine. “Children give me such strength,” she said. She also intends to speak publicly about what happened rather than remain silent.

Those signs of purpose coexist with moments of nearly disabling distress. She described crying or struggling to breathe even when, as she put it, “in my head everything is OK.”

Incidents like the confrontation with the student’s mother remind Natalia that being back at work does not mean the healing process is complete. Today, she lives in two realities: the teacher who handled a confrontation and the survivor who still experiences almost disabling flashbacks.

What Can Progress Look Like?

In her conversation with Dlugunovych, Natalia keeps asking how she can know that she has recovered. Rather than asking only whether all distress has vanished, Dlugunovych suggested looking for improvements in how she handles difficult moments in daily life.

When the mother began shouting, memories of being screamed at by soldiers still came back. Even so, Natalia was able to pause before responding. Moving the conversation to the principal’s office meant setting a boundary. She recognizes that her response was more deliberate and effective than it would have been when she first returned from captivity.

She also recognizes that being able to work and appear composed does not mean she no longer needs help. She continues taking her prescribed antidepressants and says she feels herself making progress, bit by bit, toward no longer needing them.

With Dlugunovych’s guidance, she sees that she does not have to declare herself fully recovered to recognize that she is recovering. She found particular comfort in something he said at the end of their Zoom session. They had been talking about feeling alone in the darkness of depression.

“If you find yourself alone and in the dark, it doesn’t mean you are buried,” he told her. He offered another possibility: she was planted, like a tree whose roots descend into darkness while its branches reach toward the sky. The darkness was part of her story, but it did not have to determine the direction of her growth. Natalia’s recovery is still unfolding. Steadily, she is reaching toward the light.

item.title: The Cultural Unconscious is Real
item.description:
Unconscious

The Cultural Unconscious is Real

Jungian psychology has begun reckoning with its power.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Jung remains highly influential for his notion of the collective unconscious.
  • Jungian psychology is now giving increasing attention to the cultural unconscious too.
  • The cultural unconscious affects individual as well as group, ethnic, and national behavior.
  • Therefore, it too needs to be brought into our conscious awareness.
Source: Gul Isik / Pexels

Are you acquainted with Jungian psychology or interested in exploring its intriguing ideas? If so, the collective unconscious is a vital concept. More than a century ago, Carl Jung formulated this notion based partly on his therapeutic work with psychiatric patients. Buttressed by his investigations of Eastern and Western traditions in art, folklore, and mythology, he asserted that people everywhere share the same inborn ways of experiencing the world. It was a radically unconventional concept for its time, but which Jung systematically advanced. With characteristic wit in responding to its criticisms, he stated:

"We are dealing with a generally human disposition which is instinctual and innate, as instinct is with all animals. Do you really believe that every chick invents its own way of breaking out of the egg? Or that every eel makes an individual decision to start journeying for the Bermuda Islands in the Atlantic Ocean, as though the idea was entirely new?"

What makes the collective unconscious so important, Jung argued, is that it's the source of our archetypal experiences of nature, as well as human relationships. These include love, friendship, and even warfare. "The archetypes are...dynamic," Jung wrote, "They are instinctual images that are not intellectually invented. They are always there and they produce certain processes in the unconscious that could be best compared with myths. That's the origin of mythology."

Perhaps catalyzed by the blockbuster success of the first Star Wars films, followed by literary scholar Joseph Campbell's influential TV series, The Power of Myths (with journalist Bill Moyers), the term archetype entered popular English language by the 1990s. Unfortunately, the term has often been distorted from Jung's original meaning. For example, if you peruse the Internet, you'll find many dubious websites seemingly finding archetypes everywhere--a trend which Jung foresaw decades earlier in simplistic depictions of his ideas.

The Personal Unconscious

Though Sigmund Freud never accepted Jung's work on the collective unconscious, both strongly agreed that we each have a personal unconscious that largely reflects our individual childhood experiences, especially involving our parents. For this reason, Jung always obtained a family history for every new patient. He also insisted that analytic treatment, such as dreamwork, must always uncover the patient's personal unconscious before exploring the far deeper, collective unconscious, with its timeless archetypal figures and symbolic images.

The Cultural Unconscious

For everyone interested in Jung work, it's important to know that he also identified a third, intermediary layer of our psyche. Known as the cultural unconscious, it lies between the collective unconscious that all humanity shares and the more accessible personal unconscious unique to each of us. Though Jung and his early circle said little about this intermediary realm, an exception was the Romanian scholar of religion Mircea Eliade (1907-1986). Examining cultural differences involving the archetypes, he participated actively in the annual Eranos conferences that Jung had helped to organize.

As Maslow's biographer, I discovered that he resonated strongly with Eliade's cultural research. In Religions, Values, and Peak-Experiences, Maslow applied it to such topics as healthy adolescent development, romantic love, and marriage. Alluding to Eliade's notions, Maslow suggested that pre-industrial cultures "often manage the unitive life better than we do, at least as far as relations between the sexes are concerned, and also between adults and children...(These cultures) have kept their sense of the sacred about the basic biological things of life."

Central to Jungian psychology today on the cultural unconscious has been the more recent work of Joseph Henderson (1903-2007). In such books as Shadow and Self, he argued that, whether we recognize it or not, we're unconsciously impacted by our particular culture's rites, rituals, and patterns of social interaction. These encompass family life, work, and leisure.

This impact begins in our early childhood and continues through our teenage years into adulthood. Such contemporary Jungian theorists as Thomas Singer regard the cultural unconscious as not only influencing our individual behavior, but also wider relations among ethnic groups and even entire nations. To better understand the cultural unconscious is therefore an urgent urgent task before us--bearing on social conflict versus harmony, war versus peace.

Accessing your Cultural Unconscious

To recognize our cultural unconscious is difficult, for it typically requires an act of will. It might even be compared to awakening from sleep-walking, or what the British writer Colin Wilson called the "robotic state." However, if you’ve ever traveled abroad, a remedy is available: Think back to your immediate, gut reaction when you returned to your home milieu--and what struck you as most different in the demeanor, body language, mood, and social behavior of your compatriots compared to their counterparts in the foreign country you'd just visited. In focusing on this contrast, you may catch glimpses of our cultural unconscious--and how it daily affects you.

item.title: Why Is Corporate Culture Declining in Importance?
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

Why Is Corporate Culture Declining in Importance?

Corporate culture vs. perceived institutional trust.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Corporate culture interest has dropped 90% since 2004, per Google Trends data.
  • Operational efficiency via AI is eclipsing focus on employee well-being in many firms.
  • Perceived institutional trust is now more crucial than traditional corporate culture.

Steve Gund is the CEO of a third-generation manufacturing company that has averaged 18% annual growth for a decade and zero layoffs during the same time period. The Wall Street Journal honored this accomplishment with this Page 1 headline: “Bosses Seek Secrets of Firm With No Layoffs in 75 Years.”

In this post, we will review what makes The Gund Company unique and what ideas can and cannot be utilized in your organization.

What Comes First: Revenue or Employee Well-Being?

Ed Gund started a materials company in 1951. Now approaching $400 million in annual sales, the Gund Company provides components for industrial customers such as General Electric and Rockwell Automation. According to CEO Steve Gund, the company has a culture that puts its 1,300 employees’ well-being over short-term profit. Says Gund, ”It sounds touchy-feely, but it is profitable” (Pohle, 2026).

What Does Gund Do That’s Special?

  1. Hire sparingly so employees can weather leaner times while working harder when times are good.
  2. Employees are encouraged to communicate directly with the CEO and go outside the hierarchy by writing their ideas and concerns on red cards posted around the office.
  3. Each year, every employee creates an individual development plan separate and distinct from the company compensation program. Where does the employee wish to go with his/her career, and how can the company help?
  4. Company financials are posted throughout the company. Financials involve categories including: (A) Taking Care of Business; (B) Taking Care of Customers Through On-Time Delivery and Meeting Quality Goals; (C) Taking Care of Each Other Through Low Injury Occurrences, Recognizing Peer Accomplishments, and Helping Peers Manage Personal Crisis.

"Business Structure Beats Good Intentions"

President Gund says, “We’re in the bowels of industrial manufacturing. If we can do this, anybody can do this.” Sadly, we must disagree.

The Gund Company is a privately owned company with an employee stock ownership program (ESOP) where workers own 30% of the equity. A corporate structure like this mandates boards of directors and CEOs take corporate culture seriously.

When companies go public or become private equity portfolio companies, business corporate structure beats good intentions. Owners insist on management demonstrating quarterly and yearly growth in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA). Corporate culture then takes a back seat.

There are praiseworthy exceptions like public company COSTCO, but they are rare.

An Objective Look at Corporate Culture

Google has a free public web tool called trends.google.com. It analyzes the relative popularity of search queries across Google Search, YouTube, News, Images, and Google Shopping. Search data is normalized and scored from 0 to 100 based on a term’s popularity relative to total search volume.

Between March 31 and April 30, 2004, the term “corporate culture” scored 100. In 2004, corporate culture was a “hot” topic because of the demise of energy giant Enron and Big Five CPA firm Arthur Andersen. Between March 31 and April 30, 2020, “corporate culture” dropped from 100 to 13. Between Sept. 3 and Oct. 31, 2026, “corporate culture” searches dropped to 10.

We suspect that corporate concern with maintaining and enhancing corporate culture has dropped in response to an increased obsession with enhancing operational efficiency through humans interacting with artificial intelligence (AI).

If Corporate Culture Is Not “Hot” Anymore...

In an earlier Psychology Today perspective, we suggested that as business use of AI increases, the perceived value of analytical thinking and technical competence will become more commoditized. To stand apart in a competitive marketplace, the most important thing is to be perceived by customers, prospective customers, and employees as trustworthy.

Most U.S. public companies and private equity portfolio companies are so consumed by short-term EBITDA gains that they fail to take the necessary long-range steps to generate perceived trust.

Achieving perceived institutional trust may allow some companies to adapt Gund's principles cited earlier in this post. The traditional concept of corporate culture focuses on how full-time employees treat each other and their customers. Perceived institutional trust is different in that it examines how customers/clients, full-time human employees, interim human employees, and artificial intelligence systems work together.

item.title: When Family Estrangement Comes to Work
item.description:
Career

When Family Estrangement Comes to Work

During the holidays, grief over family ruptures drains a worker's productivity.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Estrangement can affect an employee's attention and focus, disrupting attendance and output at work.
  • The massive surge in family estrangement creates a form of "brain drain" that hurts a company's bottom line.
  • Employees often bring to work estrangement issues like boundary violations, criticism, or unresolved conflict.

Every year, I notice that the mood in estrangement groups and chat rooms turns somber as Thanksgiving approaches. Many members post dark and depressed thoughts, expressing their raw emotions to strangers online. Their grieving is palpable.

Many members admit that they begin to suffer as the weather changes, and then as the holidays approach. It’s the time of year when the hurts of estrangement reach an emotional crescendo.

While I was researching my book, Brothers, Sisters, Strangers, some estranged siblings made these comments:

~ From October to December, I feel depressed and feelings of low self-worth blindside me and follow me everywhere. The holidays feed my fantasy of a loving family.

~ I dream about her and wonder if she is OK. I feel terrible about myself and I break out in hives when I talk about the estrangement.

~ I have had streaks where I cry several times a day and I wake up at night with my pillow wet. When depression overwhelms me, I don’t leave home because I’m afraid of crying in public.

Deep grief, rumination, and sleep deprivation inevitably show up at work—especially at this time of year. Robyn D. Shulman's recent article in Inc Magazine, "38 Percent of U.S. Adults Are Estranged From Family. The Workplace Is Feeling It," spotlights this overlooked phenomenon.

Estrangement can disrupt attendance and output, as well as affecting attention and ability to focus. The article asks an important question: What does it cost a person to carry a family rupture through an ordinary workday?

More estranged employees

Source: Anntarazevich/Pexels

This question is more relevant than ever as an increasing number of people are experiencing estrangements. In a 2025 YouGov poll, 38% of U.S. adults reported being estranged from at least one close family member. That number is up significantly from a 2020 Cornell University study, which found that, pre-pandemic, 27% of American adults—roughly 67 million people—were estranged from a relative.

Behind those numbers is the devastating and relentless experience of losing family members who are still alive. Many of the estranged feel they’re mourning the living. A 2024 study using data from 5,245 adults in the German Family Panel found that family estrangement, especially from both parents and siblings, was associated with lower life satisfaction and greater depression—even when a cutoff or pause in the relationship can be protective and necessary for safety.

article continues after advertisement

Estrangement goes to work

The surge in family estrangement bleeds into the professional world. In Inc, Shulman identifies several ways that estrangement functions as a distinct form of "brain drain" in the workplace:

  • The Rise of "Presenteeism." Employees who are present but absent: physically at their desks, but mentally checked out. They may be ruminating, replaying the last argument, anticipating unwanted contact, or wondering if the silence will ever end. The stress, grief, and anxiety of severing family ties drain energy, potentially causing missed deadlines, poor focus, and greater tension and irritability in the workplace.
  • Health Impacts and Absenteeism. Estrangement often causes insomnia, fatigue, and stress-related illnesses. In the workplace, these ailments may result in unexpected absences and higher healthcare costs for organizations. Research shows that chronic stress in relationships with family and friends may result in episodes of depression; ultimately, it can lead to drug and alcohol use.
  • Dysfunctional Office Dynamics. Employees often bring unresolved family traumas into professional relationships. Estrangement may result from ongoing boundary violations, criticism, betrayals and unresolved conflict. A terse message from a supervisor or exclusion from a meeting, for example, may cause a blowup, as many of these workers struggle with authority, overreact to feedback, or mismanage workplace conflict.
  • Holiday Season Triggers. In Western culture, family bonds are idealized as permanent and unconditional. Research on estrangement shows the deep stigma attached to estrangement. Workplace chats, especially surrounding holiday plans or family traditions, can be emotionally triggering. Estranged workers, who often feel shame, may become more anxious and depressed. Some may cope by withdrawing, possibly leading to lower morale for everyone.

What employees can do

Manage Workload

  • Talk to your supervisor: Schedule a check-in to clarify expectations, discuss priorities, or explore flexible scheduling options.
  • Prioritize tasks: Break projects into small steps, and drop or postpone non-essential meetings and tasks.
  • Set boundaries: Communicate your availability, and say no to non-critical assignments. Avoid checking personal email during the workday and don't answer calls at work that might upset you.

Reset Focus During the Workday

  • Take breaks: Step away from your desk for short walks, fresh air, or coffee.
  • Unplug from distractions: Limit personal holiday shopping, messaging, or social media scrolling during work hours. Limit time spent on social media, as many post photos of idealized family gatherings that can cause distress.
  • Practice grounding techniques: Use deep breathing exercises and mindfulness when you feel agitated.
  • Switch to highly engaging tasks: Move away from passive, repetitive work that allows your mind to wander. Focus on tasks requiring intense concentration, logic, or collaboration.
  • Narrate your actions: To keep your mind on the immediate task, tell yourself exactly what you are focusing on now (e.g., "I am reading this report. I am writing this email").
article continues after advertisement

Recharge at home

  • Use your Paid Time Off (PTO): Disconnect from work when using paid time off for a mental break. Leave home stress at home and work stress at work.
  • Maintain healthy habits: Prioritize sleep, balanced meals, and regular physical activity to balance yourself.
  • Seek support: Reach out to your supportive community -- coworkers, friends, family. Create new holiday rituals that offer safety and belonging.
  • Schedule "worry time": Give yourself 10 minutes to think about the situation, and discipline yourself to save worrisome thoughts for that time.
  • Use emotional writing as narrative therapy. Validate your grief in writing. Then, if you’d like, shred the paper to signal to your brain that you’re done with those thoughts for now.

These measures can reduce the cost of estrangement at work, and they may help employees keep their jobs.

item.title: Taurine: An Overlooked Amino Acid for Mental Health
item.description:
Psychopharmacology

Taurine: An Overlooked Amino Acid for Mental Health

The calming nutrient listed on energy drinks may help some psychiatric conditions.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Taurine acts like a brake in the brain, activating the same calming receptors as GABA and glycine.
  • Taurine added to antipsychotic medication reduced symptoms in young people with first-episode psychosis (FEP).
  • Animal studies suggest taurine may ease depression, anxiety, and ADHD-like behavior.
  • Taurine blocks the same NMDA receptor as ketamine, suggesting it may have antidepressant properties.

If you've heard of taurine, it's probably because you saw it listed under the ingredients on the back of an energy drink. But taurine isn't a stimulant. In fact, its effects on the brain are almost the opposite.

Taurine is one of the most abundant amino acids in the brain. But unlike most amino acids, it isn't used to build proteins. Instead, it helps cells balance salt and water, protects them from oxidative stress, and supports mitochondria, which are the energy factories inside our cells. In 2023, researchers reported in Science that blood taurine levels fall with age in humans, and that taurine supplements extended the healthy lifespan of animals. That study triggered a wave of public interest and raised the question: Can taurine help the brain?

The Brain's Brake Pedal

Our brains run on a balance between excitatory “go” signals and inhibitory “stop” signals. Glutamate is the primary accelerator, while GABA and glycine are the main brakes. Taurine is shaped much like GABA and can activate GABA-A and glycine receptors, thereby reducing the firing of nerve cells.

Taurine and GABA
Source: Claude.ai generated image

Taurine also blocks NMDA receptors, which are the same glutamate receptors that are blocked by ketamine. This is an interesting and important finding that suggests taurine might function like ketamine in terms of helping with depression.

Taurine and Ketamine
Source: Claude.ai generated image

Many psychiatric conditions involve an imbalance between the glutamate and GABA/glycine systems. This has led researchers to wonder if taurine could help with these conditions.

Psychosis: The Strongest Human Evidence

The best human evidence comes from a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in young people experiencing their first episode of psychosis. Researchers in Australia randomly assigned patients aged 18 to 25 who were taking low-dose antipsychotic medication to receive either 4 grams of taurine or a placebo daily for 12 weeks. Among the 86 people analyzed, taurine significantly reduced overall psychiatric symptoms as well as psychotic symptoms. Depressive symptoms and everyday functioning also improved. Taurine was well tolerated.

Curiously, blood taurine levels are higher in people who are experiencing their first episode of psychosis and have not been treated with antipsychotic medications. Their taurine levels return to normal after they are treated with antipsychotic medication. This may reflect the body’s attempt to calm overactive brain circuits. These studies suggest taurine may improve symptoms of psychosis.

Depression

Most of the research exploring the effects of taurine on depression has been performed in animals, not humans. For example, in rats exposed to weeks of mild stress (which is a common laboratory model of depression), taurine prevented the loss of interest in sugar water (a sign of anhedonia or the inability to feel pleasure), protected memory, and promoted the growth of new neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region that shrinks when we are depressed. Another study involved feeding rats a high-taurine diet for four weeks. These rats exhibited antidepressant-like behavior.

In humans, the picture is more complex. People with untreated major depression have been found to have higher blood taurine levels than non-depressed controls. A recent systematic review of human studies found inconsistent effects of taurine on mood.

Anxiety

Because taurine activates calming receptors, it would appear logical that it might reduce anxiety. In mice, a single oral dose of taurine reduced anxiety-like behavior without causing impairment in memory or muscle function. The researchers attributed taurine’s anti-anxiety effects to activation of glycine receptors. A similar effect occurred when taurine was administered to mice intranasally.

But here’s a twist. A different mouse study found that whereas a single injection of taurine reduced anxiety, drinking taurine in water chronically increased anxiety. It’s possible that the brain adapts to chronic taurine exposure in a way that is different from administering a single dose. Also, injecting taurine may produce different results than drinking it.

ADHD

The evidence for ADHD is still in a preliminary stage. Spontaneously hypertensive rats are a commonly used animal model of ADHD. In these animals, dietary taurine lowered inflammatory markers, changed brain activity on functional MRI, and improved working memory. High-dose taurine also changed how the brain handled dopamine, the chemical messenger that is targeted by stimulant medications such as methylphenidate. Low-dose taurine had the opposite effect on dopamine, suggesting that the dose matters. No human ADHD trials have been published so far.

Is Taurine Safe?

Taurine has a good safety record. A review of human studies found that 3 grams per day is a safe level for healthy adults, although higher amounts, such as the 4-gram dose in the psychosis trial mentioned above, have been used in research without serious problems. The FDA has accepted taurine as generally recognized as safe (GRAS) as a food ingredient, and diets that include meat and seafood provide about 400 milligrams a day. Side effects are uncommon but can include an upset stomach.

One important caution – energy drinks are not a good way to get taurine. Their caffeine and sugar can worsen anxiety and disrupt sleep.

The Bottom Line

Taurine is a promising, inexpensive, and generally safe supplement that acts on the brain’s calming systems. The best human evidence supports it as an add-on treatment for early psychosis. For depression, anxiety, and ADHD, most of the evidence comes from animals. If you’re interested in trying taurine, discuss it with your doctor first, especially if you take psychiatric medications. Taurine should complement, not replace, proven treatments.

item.title: When Porn Becomes Sex Education, What Happens in College?
item.description:
Pornography

When Porn Becomes Sex Education, What Happens in College?

How pornography shapes sexual behavior and expectations.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Pornography is shaping many young people's expectations about sex, intimacy, and consent.
  • Exposure to violent pornography is associated with lower empathy and greater acceptance of sexual coercion.
  • Teens need to understand how peer attitudes and emotional desensitization can reinforce sexual coercion.

It was Halloween night. A college freshman went with friends to a fraternity party, hoping to see a sophomore boy she liked. They flirted and he invited her to his dorm room. She agreed to go.

They started kissing and he pushed her down on the bed, wanting to go further. She said, “No, I don't want to do this." He continued. Despite her words and attempts to push him away, he raped her.

Later, she learned that other women had similar experiences with the same student yet she was the first to formally report the assault. He apparently disregarded clearly expressed sexual boundaries multiple times.

Recent national allegations of sexual assaults on college campuses, degrading group messages, and bystanders enabling abusive behavior raise troubling questions about male sexual entitlement and peer culture. What leads some young men to disregard another person's refusal or inability to consent? Where is empathy in these encounters? And what role might pornography play in shaping young people's understanding of intimacy, pleasure, consent, and power?

What Is Pornography Teaching?

Today's college students grew up with pornography available within seconds, often before their first romantic relationship. A national survey found that 73% of teenagers, ages 13 to 17, had viewed online pornography, with the average age of first exposure at 12 (Robb & Mann, 2023). Among those who viewed pornography, 45% of teens believed it provided “helpful information about sex” (Robb & Mann, 2023).

What exactly are young people learning from pornography?

The same survey found that 52% of teenagers who had viewed pornography reported seeing violent or aggressive content, including depictions of apparent rape, sexual strangulation, or someone in pain (Robb & Mann, 2023). Other researchers examined 255 popular pornography videos from 2000 through 2024 and found physical aggression in approximately 44% of the videos (Shor and Liu, 2026). Aggressive incidents nearly tripled between the earliest and latest decades studied with significant increases in spanking, hitting, and sexual choking (Shor & Liu, 2026). We have to wonder how seeing these behaviors on screen impacts what young adults believe to be “normal” or arousing. Without opportunities to question pornographic portrayals, young people may incorporate some of these messages, or scripts, into their developing sexual expectations.

Pornography and Empathy

A 2026 review of seven studies examined the relationship between pornography use and empathy (Hernández-Monferrer et al., 2026). One of these experimental studies linked exposure to films depicting sexual violence against women with reduced sympathy toward sexual assault victims (Linz et al., 1988). More recent research involving 3,607 Spanish young adults linked violent pornography exposure with lower empathy among men and greater acceptance of violence against women among both men and women (Sanz-Barbero et al., 2025). Although the evidence cannot establish that pornography decreased empathy, these findings raise concerns about emotional desensitization following repeated exposure.

Empathy allows us to recognize and respond with care to another person and their feelings. In contrast, sexual objectification reduces a person to an instrument of gratification. Modern pornography highlights these dynamics when humiliation or resistance are eroticized, and another person's discomfort is ignored.

Importantly, the 2026 review found that higher empathy was associated with lower sexual violence perpetration, suggesting that empathy may play a protective role (Hernández-Monferrer et al., 2026).

From Sexual Scripts to Sexual Coercion

Another pivotal study followed 247 college men over seven months, examining how violent pornography exposure impacted attitudes and behavior (Bhuptani et al., 2025). The researchers found that greater exposure to violent pornography was associated with more gender-inequitable attitudes, greater alcohol-related problems, and less responsibility assigned to men who commit rape (Bhuptani et al., 2025). These factors helped explain the relationship between violent pornography exposure and increased self-reported sexually coercive behavior seven months later (Bhuptani et al., 2025). The study cannot establish cause and effect, but the connection between beliefs and later assaultive behavior deserves serious attention.

Peer influence adds to these risks. In an earlier study of 283 college men, Bhuptani and colleagues (2024) found that believing peers approved of pornography depicting rape was associated with more negative attitudes toward women. Perceived peer acceptance of rape pornography was the only factor that remained significant after accounting for other variables examined.

It is likely that what young men believe their friends approve of is important. When degrading comments or images generate laughter, or someone ignores another person's boundaries without challenge, silence can communicate acceptance.

Empathy Education Is Essential

Parents may prepare teenagers for college by discussing alcohol, drugs, dating, and personal safety. But how many ask what their children have learned about sex and relationships from pornography?

According to Robb and Mann (2023), 57% of teenagers surveyed had never discussed pornography with a trusted adult. As a marriage and family therapist, I believe these conversations need to begin long before college on a regular basis. Simply knowing the definition of consent does not guarantee that someone will respect another person's boundaries. Young people need opportunities to develop and practice empathy, communication skills, mutual respect, and accountability. We can also teach young people how to respond and challenge peers who share sexual images or trivialize coercion.

Parents and mentors can help by asking questions about the relationships portrayed in pornography and other media. Are both people treated as individuals with feelings and choices? What happens when someone appears uncomfortable, unwilling, or unable to consent? What does a healthy, caring relationship look like?

Programs like iempathize empower youth and adults with empathy training to eradicate exploitation. School and home-based initiatives that inspire insight and action are promising prevention approaches worthy of further research.

The young woman in that dorm room clearly said "no." We cannot know whether pornography influenced the young man who sexually assaulted her. But the research gives us compelling reasons to examine the sexual messages young people absorb and the attitudes their peers reinforce. If pornography is helping shape how young people understand sex, how can we intervene, as parents and mentors, and teach them empathy, love, care, and respect?
